question: Slovák, ktorý sa vyberie na veľký nákup do Rakúska, môže naraziť na zatvorené dvere takmer všetkých obchodov. V ktorý deň v týždni sa mu to stane?
source_excerpt: Stores are generally not allowed to be open on Sundays and public holidays, with the law on shop opening hours stipulating that only certain categories of stores may operate.

extra.why_interesting: Slovaks are used to malls being open all weekend and may assume a big rich neighbour works the same way. Many have actually driven to Austria and found shops shut, so they can work out the answer, and the Parndorf detail is the surprising payoff.
extra.verification_notes: Austrian Öffnungszeitengesetz generally bars shop opening on Sundays and public holidays, and I found no 2026 change (https://thelocal.at/20220422/why-everything-in-austria-is-closed-on-sundays-and-what-to-do-instead/).

explanation: Rakúsky zákon nariaďuje, aby boli obchody v nedeľu zatvorené. Výnimku majú len obchody na staniciach, letiskách a pumpách, takže v nedeľu je zatvorený aj obľúbený outlet v Parndorfe.

question: Keď Slováci nakupujú v Maďarsku, platia forintmi. Názov tejto meny pochádza z mena jedného talianskeho mesta. Ktorého?
source_excerpt: The name comes from Florence, Italy, where gold coins called fiorino d'oro were minted from 1252.

extra.why_interesting: Slovaks shopping in Hungary handle forints all the time without wondering where the name comes from. The sound of 'forint' is close to 'Florencia', so a player can reason their way to the answer and enjoy the moment it clicks.
extra.verification_notes: The forint is named after Florence's gold fiorino; Hungary still uses the forint with no euro adoption date set (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_forint).

explanation: Vo Florencii sa v stredoveku razila zlatá minca fiorino, ktorá platila po celej Európe. Uhorsko podľa nej pomenovalo vlastné mince, a tak sa dnes na Balatone platí menou nazvanou po Florencii.
